Title: The Extra Change
Dilemma: You buy a snack at the store. The cashier is in a hurry and gives you a ten-dollar bill back instead of a one-dollar bill. Nobody noticed, and you could really use the money.
Question: Is it okay to keep the extra money, since it was the cashier's mistake and not yours?
Right Choice: Return the money
Wrong Choice: Keep the money
Catholic Answer: No. Keeping money you know is not yours is a form of taking what belongs to someone else, even if you did nothing to cause the mistake. The Catechism lists knowingly keeping what is not ours, such as lost objects or money given in error, as a sin against the Seventh Commandment. The cashier may even have to pay back the missing money out of their own pocket. The right thing to do is to point out the mistake and give back the extra money right away. Honesty in small things builds the habit of honesty in big things (Luke 16:10).
Key Principle: Justice: give each person what is rightfully theirs; we may not keep what we know belongs to another.
Sources: CCC 2409 (Holy See): https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P8B.HTM

Title: The Lost Wallet
Dilemma: Walking home from school, you find a wallet on the sidewalk with forty dollars and a driver's license inside. Your friend says, "Finders keepers! Nobody will ever know."
Question: Do you have to try to return it, or can you keep what you found?
Right Choice: Return the wallet to its owner
Wrong Choice: Keep the wallet and the cash
Catholic Answer: You must make a real effort to return it. A lost item still belongs to its owner, and the Catechism names the "deliberate retention of... objects lost" as a sin against the Seventh Commandment (CCC 2409). Here the owner can be identified from the license, so the duty is clear: return it yourself with a parent, or hand it to the police or another responsible adult who can reach the owner. While the owner can be found, keeping the wallet or the cash is never right. Returning it is also an act of love for a neighbor who is probably worried.
Key Principle: Lost property still belongs to its owner; justice requires a real effort to return it.
Sources: The Wanderer, "Accounting to St. Peter": https://thewandererpress.com/catholic/news/frontpage/accounting-to-st-peter/ ; Opus Dei, Topic 36: Seventh Commandment: https://opusdei.org/en/article/topic-36-seventh-commandment/

Title: Can I Copy Your Homework?
Dilemma: Your best friend forgot to do the math homework and begs to copy yours before class. If you say no, your friend will be upset and might get a bad grade.
Question: Is letting a friend copy your work a kind thing to do, or is it wrong?
Right Choice: Say no, and offer to help your friend learn it
Wrong Choice: Let your friend copy your homework
Catholic Answer: Letting a friend copy is not truly kind, because it helps them deceive the teacher and pass off your work as their own. Cheating is a form of dishonesty and unfairness to the teacher and to the other students who did the work. When we help someone else do something wrong, we share in their wrongdoing. Real friendship wants what is truly good for the other person, so you could offer to help your friend understand the problems at lunch, or encourage them to be honest with the teacher. Saying no kindly is an act of love.
Key Principle: Truthfulness and justice; we may not help others sin, and real charity wills the true good of another.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Ugly Sweater
Dilemma: Your grandmother knitted you a sweater for your birthday. You think it is ugly and scratchy. She smiles and asks, "Do you love it?"
Question: Should you tell a "white lie" and say you love it, to spare her feelings?
Right Choice: Thank her truthfully for her love and hard work
Wrong Choice: Tell her you love the sweater
Catholic Answer: The Church teaches that lying, which is speaking a falsehood in order to deceive, is wrong by its very nature, though small lies are usually venial sins and not mortal ones. But honesty does not require being rude. You can say true and loving things: you love that she made it for you, you can see how much work went into it, and you are grateful she thought of you. Charity and respect for the truth should guide every answer we give. With a little thought, we can almost always find something both true and kind to say.
Key Principle: Never lie, but speak the truth with charity and tact.
Sources: OSV, "Are little white lies okay to tell?": https://www.oursundayvisitor.com/are-little-white-lies-okay-to-tell/ ; Catholic Encyclopedia, "Lying": https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/lying

Title: The Surprise Party
Dilemma: Your family is planning a surprise party for your mom. She notices you whispering and asks, "What are you all up to?"
Question: How do you keep the surprise without telling a lie?
Right Choice: Say it's a secret, or change the subject
Wrong Choice: Make up a false story to cover it
Catholic Answer: Keeping a good secret is not the same as lying. The Catechism teaches that we are not always required to reveal everything we know, and that we may keep silent or use discreet language when there is a good reason. You might say, "It's a secret, you'll find out soon!" or simply change the subject with a smile. What you should avoid is making up a false story, like saying you were talking about homework. A happy surprise is a good reason to keep quiet, and it can be done without deceiving anyone.
Key Principle: We may keep silent or be discreet for a good reason, but we may not deceive by lying.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Is Lying a Sin if Done to Protect Someone from Death?" (discussion of CCC 2488-2489): https://www.catholic.com/qa/is-lying-a-sin-if-done-to-protect-someone-from-death

Title: The Sunday Tournament
Dilemma: Your soccer team made it to the championship tournament. The final game is Sunday morning, at the same time as Mass, and the coach says everyone must be there.
Question: Is a big game a good enough reason to miss Sunday Mass?
Right Choice: Go to a Mass that fits, even if it means missing the game
Wrong Choice: Skip Mass to play the game
Catholic Answer: Sunday Mass is a serious obligation: the faithful must take part "unless excused for a serious reason (for example, illness, the care of infants) or dispensed by their own pastor," and "those who deliberately fail in this obligation commit a grave sin" (CCC 2181). A game is a choice, not an inability, so it is not by itself a reason to miss Mass. The obligation is to take part in Mass on the Sunday or holy day, not at one particular time, so there is usually a way to do both: a Saturday evening vigil Mass fulfills the obligation (CCC 2180), or there may be a Mass near the tournament at another time. If you truly cannot get to any Mass for reasons beyond your control, you are not at fault. But if the only obstacle is the game, put God first. Making the effort is also a strong witness to your teammates.
Key Principle: Keep holy the Lord's Day; Sunday Mass comes before games and entertainment.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Missing Mass on a Sunday or Other Holy Day of Obligation": https://www.catholic.com/qa/missing-mass-on-a-holy-day-of-obligation ; The Catholic Spirit, "When sports clash with Sunday Mass": https://thecatholicspirit.com/special-sections/back-to-school/sports-clash-sunday-mass-whats-parent/

Title: The Bystander
Dilemma: At recess, some kids are making fun of a classmate and knocking his books down. You are not joining in, but you are afraid that if you step in, they will pick on you next.
Question: If you are not the one doing the bullying, have you done anything wrong by just watching?
Right Choice: Get a teacher or other adult to help, and befriend him
Wrong Choice: Stay quiet and just watch
Catholic Answer: Staying silent can make us share in someone else's wrongdoing: we are responsible for others' sins when we cooperate in them, including "by not disclosing or not hindering them when we have an obligation to do so" (CCC 1868). You are not required to confront the bullies yourself or put yourself in danger. But silence is not the only alternative. Refuse to laugh along, get a teacher or another responsible adult involved right away, and be a friend to the classmate afterward, by sitting with him or helping pick up his books. Not stepping in one particular way is different from knowingly helping the bullying continue by laughing, cheering, or joining in. Comforting those who suffer is one of the works of mercy (CCC 2447).
Key Principle: Love of neighbor: take safe, proportionate action, and never help bullying continue.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: Is it Gossip if it is True?
Dilemma: You find out that a classmate got caught shoplifting last summer. Some friends ask if you know anything juicy about her. You say, "Well, it's true, so it's not really gossip."
Question: If something bad about a person is true, is it okay to tell others?
Right Choice: Keep her past to yourself
Wrong Choice: Tell your friends what she did
Catholic Answer: No. Telling others about someone's real faults or sins without a good and serious reason is a sin called detraction. Even when it is true, it hurts the person's good name, which is very hard to repair. If the story is false, it is even worse, a sin called calumny. A good reason to share might be keeping someone safe, such as telling a parent or teacher about danger, but not entertaining friends. We should speak about others the way we would want them to speak about us.
Key Principle: Respect for every person's reputation; we may not reveal another's faults without a valid reason.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Dangerous Secret
Dilemma: Your close friend tells you she has been hurting herself, and makes you promise not to tell anyone, especially not an adult.
Question: Should you keep the promise, or break it to get her help?
Right Choice: Tell a trusted adult so she gets help
Wrong Choice: Keep the promise and tell no one
Catholic Answer: If she may be in immediate danger, get help right away: tell a parent, teacher, or other responsible adult at once, or call emergency services (in the U.S., 911, or call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). A promise of secrecy never outweighs protecting a life. Normally we should keep secrets that others trust us with, but the Catechism teaches that a confidence need not be kept "where keeping the secret is bound to cause very grave harm to the one who confided it, to the one who received it or to a third party" (CCC 2491). Even when she is not in immediate danger, tell a trusted adult such as a parent, school counselor, or priest as soon as possible, even if she is upset at first. Keep being her friend, pray for her, and let her know you told because you care about her.
Key Principle: Secrets must be kept, except when keeping them would cause very grave harm; a life in danger comes first.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Heinz Dilemma
Dilemma: A man's wife is dying, and only one expensive drug can save her. The druggist who invented it charges ten times what it costs to make. The man begs for a lower price or a payment plan, but is refused. In desperation, he breaks in and steals the drug.
Question: Was he wrong to steal the drug to save his wife's life?
Right Choice: Exhaust every other way first; take it only if it is truly the last way to save her
Wrong Choice: Let her die, because the druggist's profit comes first
Catholic Answer: The Catechism teaches that there is no theft "in obvious and urgent necessity when the only way to provide for immediate, essential needs (food, shelter, clothing...) is to put at one's disposal and use the property of others" (CCC 2408). That is a narrow principle, not a blanket permission, and everything depends on the facts. Is her life truly in immediate danger? Is taking the drug really the only way left? He must first try every reasonable alternative: other doctors and hospitals, the parish, charities, public assistance, and the community. Only if all of these truly fail and her life is at stake could his act fall under that principle, and whether it does in a real case depends on how immediate and serious the need is and on all the circumstances. Even then he should, as far as he is able, make things right with the druggist afterward. The druggist also does wrong: the Catechism condemns "forcing up prices by taking advantage of the ignorance or hardship of another" (CCC 2409).
Key Principle: The universal destination of goods: urgent necessity can change what counts as theft, but only when every other way has failed.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "A Moral Assessment of 'The Heinz Dilemma'": https://www.catholic.com/qa/a-moral-assessment-of-the-heinz-dilemma

Title: The Intruder
Dilemma: In the middle of the night, an armed intruder breaks into your home and threatens your family. The only way to stop him may be to seriously injure or even kill him.
Question: Is it a sin to use deadly force to defend yourself and your family?
Right Choice: Defend your family, using only the force needed to stop him
Wrong Choice: Do whatever you want to him; he deserves it
Catholic Answer: Not when the force is truly needed. The Church teaches that legitimate defense can be morally justified, and that for those responsible for others, like a parent, it can be a serious duty. Following St. Thomas Aquinas, the act has two effects: protecting life and harming the attacker. The goal must be to stop the attack, not to kill for its own sake. A person must use only as much force as is needed, so if the intruder can be stopped by lesser means, those should be used. Whether a particular response is justified depends on the threat and the force used. As the Catechism puts it, "If a man in self-defense uses more than necessary violence, it will be unlawful: whereas if he repels force with moderation, his defense will be lawful" (CCC 2264).
Key Principle: Legitimate defense; love for oneself and duty to protect others, using only necessary force.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Confession of a Crime
Dilemma: A man confesses to a priest that he committed a terrible crime. Another person has been arrested and blamed for it. The priest is the only one who knows the truth.
Question: Should the priest go to the police to free the innocent person?
Right Choice: Keep the seal, and urge the man to turn himself in
Wrong Choice: Tell the police what the man confessed
Catholic Answer: No. "Every priest who hears confessions is bound under very severe penalties to keep absolute secrecy regarding the sins that his penitents have confessed to him.... This secret, which admits of no exceptions, is called the 'sacramental seal'" (CCC 1467). Under the Code of Canon Law, a confessor who directly violates the seal incurs an automatic (latae sententiae) excommunication reserved to the Apostolic See (can. 1386 §1). The seal protects every person's freedom to confess sins to God without fear. The priest may not disclose anything he heard, but he can urge the penitent to take responsibility: to turn himself in, free the innocent person, and make things right, and he may offer to help him do so. According to Catholic Answers, the priest may not refuse absolution to force the person to go to the police, though he may withhold it if the penitent is not truly sorry.
Key Principle: The sacramental seal of confession is inviolable.
Sources: Code of Canon Law, can. 1386 (Holy See): https://www.vatican.va/archive/cod-iuris-canonici/eng/documents/cic_lib6-cann1364-1399_en.html ; Catholic Answers, "Can Absolution Be Withheld from a Murderer Until He Agrees to Give Himself Up?": https://www.catholic.com/qa/can-absolution-be-withheld-from-a-murderer-until-he-agrees-to-give-himself-up-to-authorities ; Catholic Answers, "Priestly Responsibility Regarding Crimes Confessed": https://www.catholic.com/qa/priestly-responsibility-regarding-crimes-confessed

Title: The Boss's Request
Dilemma: You have a part-time job. Your manager asks you to change the dates on expired food labels so the store does not lose money. He says it is "company policy" and you could lose your job if you refuse.
Question: If your boss orders it, are you still responsible?
Right Choice: Refuse, even if it costs you the job
Wrong Choice: Change the labels as ordered
Catholic Answer: Yes. Following orders does not excuse us from doing something wrong. Falsifying labels is fraud and could make customers sick, which is a serious injustice. Directly carrying out a wrong act yourself, or sharing in the wrongdoer's intention, is never allowed. The Catechism teaches that we must always obey the certain judgment of a well-formed conscience. You should respectfully refuse, explain why, and, if needed, report the problem to someone higher up, even if it costs you the job. God sees and rewards those who choose integrity.
Key Principle: Never formally cooperate in evil; obey a well-formed conscience over unjust orders.
Sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, "Accomplice" (formal and material cooperation): https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/accomplice ; National Catholic Bioethics Center, "The Courage to Refuse to Cooperate in Evil": https://www.ncbcenter.org/making-sense-of-bioethics-cms/column-070-the-courage-to-refuse-to-cooperate-in-evil

Title: The Kidney for a Brother
Dilemma: Your older brother's kidneys are failing. Tests show that you are a perfect match. Doctors say you can live a healthy life with one kidney, but surgery always has some risk.
Question: Is it right to give away part of your own body, and are you required to?
Right Choice: Donate freely as a gift of love, if you prayerfully choose to
Wrong Choice: Refuse, because giving away part of your body is a sin
Catholic Answer: Donating an organ while alive can be a beautiful act of generous love. The Catechism teaches that "organ transplants are in conformity with the moral law if the physical and psychological dangers and risks to the donor are proportionate to the good that is sought for the recipient" (CCC 2296). In practice that means two things. First, the donor must understand the risks and give free, explicit consent: no one may be forced or pressured. Second, the risk to the donor must be weighed honestly, with the doctors, against the good it does. Living with one healthy kidney is a risk many donors can reasonably accept. But no one may give an organ in a way that would directly cause his own death or seriously disable him, such as giving a heart. Because it is an act of charity and not a strict obligation, a person may prayerfully decide either way. Selling organs is never allowed.
Key Principle: Organ donation is a noble gift when the risk is proportionate and consent is free.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Ticking Bomb
Dilemma: Police have captured a terrorist who planted a bomb somewhere in a city. It will explode in a few hours and kill thousands. He refuses to say where it is. An officer suggests torturing him to get the information.
Question: Can torture be justified if it might save thousands of lives?
Right Choice: Refuse to torture him; use only lawful means
Wrong Choice: Torture him to find the bomb
Catholic Answer: No. The Catechism teaches that torture, which uses physical or moral violence to extract confessions, punish, frighten, or satisfy hatred, is contrary to respect for human dignity. St. John Paul II listed torture among acts that are intrinsically evil, which means they can never be justified by good intentions or good results. The U.S. bishops have taught the same, calling torture intrinsically evil. Even a guilty person keeps the dignity of a child of God. Society must use every legitimate means, but never evil means, to protect innocent life.
Key Principle: Some acts are intrinsically evil and can never be done, whatever the consequences.
Sources: USCCB, "Torture is an Intrinsic Evil": https://www.usccb.org/resources/torture-intrinsic-evil-catholic-study-guide-one-session-workshop ; USCCB, "Background on Torture": https://www.usccb.org/resources/background-torture-february-2013

Title: The Ventilator
Dilemma: Your grandfather has terminal cancer and is now on a ventilator. Doctors say the machine will not cure him and only prolongs his dying, which is causing him great burden. Your family must decide whether to remove it.
Question: Would removing the ventilator be the same as euthanasia?
Right Choice: Remove the ventilator, but keep caring for him
Wrong Choice: Give him a lethal dose to end it faster
Catholic Answer: No. Euthanasia is choosing to cause death in order to end suffering, and it is always wrong (CCC 2277). Stopping a treatment is different when the treatment itself has become "burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary, or disproportionate to the expected outcome" (CCC 2278). Here the ventilator cannot cure him and only prolongs his dying at great burden. Removing it does not aim at his death: "one's inability to impede it is merely accepted" (CCC 2278). The decision belongs to him if he is able to make it, or otherwise to those legally entitled to act for him. What must continue is the ordinary care owed to every sick person (CCC 2279): comfort, cleanliness, pain relief, and company. Food and water are, in principle, part of that basic care, and should be given as long as his body can take them in and they benefit him rather than adding serious burden; that judgment is made with the doctors. The family should also call a priest for the sacraments.
Key Principle: Treatment that is excessively burdensome or offers little benefit may be stopped; basic care and comfort must continue.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Church Teaching on End-of-Life Care": https://www.catholic.com/qa/church-teaching-on-end-of-life-care ; National Catholic Bioethics Center, "Turning Off a Ventilator versus Withdrawing Assisted Nutrition and Hydration": https://www.ncbcenter.org/messages-from-presidents/turningoffaventilator

Title: "Please Help Me Die"
Dilemma: An elderly woman with a painful illness lives in a place where assisted suicide is legal. She tells her family she does not want to be a burden and asks them to support her request for a lethal prescription.
Question: Is it merciful to help someone end their life to stop their suffering?
Right Choice: Stay with her and get her good pain care
Wrong Choice: Help her get the lethal prescription
Catholic Answer: No. The Church teaches that any act or omission that by itself or by intention causes death in order to end suffering is a grave offense against the dignity of the person and against God. True mercy means staying with the suffering person, not eliminating them. This is not the same as refusing or stopping medical treatment: stopping procedures that are "burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary, or disproportionate to the expected outcome can be legitimate," because it accepts death rather than causing it (CCC 2278). Palliative care is encouraged: doctors may give strong painkillers to relieve pain, even if they might shorten life, as long as death is not intended. The family can reassure her that she is loved and never a burden, and help her receive the sacraments.
Key Principle: Life is a gift from God; euthanasia and assisted suicide are never permitted, but pain relief is.
Sources: Catholic Answers, "Church Teaching on End-of-Life Care": https://www.catholic.com/qa/church-teaching-on-end-of-life-care

Title: The Unjust Order
Dilemma: A soldier at war is ordered by his commander to open fire on a village full of unarmed civilians as punishment for an enemy attack. Refusing could mean being arrested or worse.
Question: Is a soldier guilty if he is only following orders?
Right Choice: Refuse to fire on the civilians
Wrong Choice: Obey the order and fire
Catholic Answer: Yes. The Catechism teaches that actions deliberately contrary to the law of nations, and the orders that command them, are crimes, and that blind obedience does not excuse those who carry them out. Deliberately killing non-combatants is always gravely wrong. The soldier has a duty to refuse, even at great personal cost. Citizens and soldiers are obliged in conscience not to follow commands that are contrary to the moral order.
Key Principle: Moral law binds even in war; unjust orders must be refused.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Lifeboat
Dilemma: After a shipwreck, a lifeboat built for ten people holds twelve, and it is starting to sink. Someone suggests throwing two of the weakest passengers overboard so the rest can survive.
Question: May the group sacrifice two people to save ten?
Right Choice: Refuse to throw anyone overboard
Wrong Choice: Throw the two weakest overboard
Catholic Answer: No. Throwing innocent people overboard would be directly killing them, which is always gravely wrong no matter how many lives might be saved. We may never do evil so that good may come of it. However, a person may freely choose to give up his own place out of love, which is very different from killing. Jesus said that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. St. Maximilian Kolbe did this at Auschwitz when he offered his life in place of another prisoner.
Key Principle: Direct killing of the innocent is never allowed, but freely laying down one's own life out of love is heroic.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Jury Room
Dilemma: You serve on a jury in a murder trial and the defendant is clearly guilty of a terrible crime. Now the jury must choose between life in prison and the death penalty.
Question: What does the Church teach about the death penalty today?
Right Choice: Weigh it in conscience, guided by the Church's teaching, which favors life in prison
Wrong Choice: Vote for the death penalty
Catholic Answer: In 2018, Pope Francis revised the Catechism to teach that "the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person," and that the Church works for its abolition worldwide (CCC 2267, as revised). Modern prisons can protect society while still giving the guilty a chance to repent. This does not mean the crime is unimportant: legitimate authority has "the right and the duty to inflict punishment proportionate to the gravity of the offense" (CCC 2266), and victims deserve care. That is the Church's moral teaching. A juror also has legal duties, which depend on the jurisdiction. In the United States, for example, potential jurors in a capital case are asked about their views on the death penalty during jury selection, and must answer truthfully. A Catholic in that position should be honest about his convictions, and, if seated, form his vote in conscience, taking account of the law and the judge's instructions. The Church's teaching points toward a just punishment such as life in prison that protects the public while respecting human dignity, but the decision belongs to the juror's well-formed conscience, not to a formula.
Key Principle: Every human life, even the guilty, has dignity; punishment must protect society without taking life.
Sources: CCC 2267 as revised in 2018 (Holy See): https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20180801_catechismo-penadimorte_en.html ; USCCB statements on the death penalty

Title: The Ectopic Pregnancy
Dilemma: A young mother learns that her pregnancy is ectopic: her baby has implanted in her fallopian tube instead of her uterus. The baby cannot survive there, and the tube may burst and cause life-threatening bleeding. Doctors recommend surgery to remove the damaged part of the tube, and the baby will not survive.
Question: Is removing the damaged tube the same as an abortion?
Right Choice: Remove the damaged tube to save the mother's life
Wrong Choice: Refuse the surgery, since it is the same as an abortion
Catholic Answer: No. Direct abortion, "willed either as an end or a means, is gravely contrary to the moral law" (CCC 2271), and the U.S. bishops' Ethical and Religious Directives state: "In case of extrauterine pregnancy, no intervention is morally licit which constitutes a direct abortion" (Directive 48). The directive does not list which treatments meet that standard. Many Catholic moral theologians, as the Catholic Health Association reports, hold that removing the damaged section of the tube (a salpingectomy) to save the mother's life can be morally licit under the principle of double effect: the surgery treats the mother's life-threatening condition, and the baby's death is foreseen but not intended, nor the means by which the mother is saved. Whether other treatments, such as the drug methotrexate or removing only the embryo while leaving the tube in place, are permissible is disputed among faithful Catholic ethicists, and real cases need careful medical and moral evaluation with specialists. In every case the baby is a real person to be loved, mourned, and prayed for.
Key Principle: Double effect distinguishes treating a deadly condition, with a tragic side effect, from directly taking an innocent life.
Sources: USCCB, Ethical and Religious Directives for Catholic Health Care Services, Directive 48; Catholic Voice (Archdiocese of Omaha), "Dispelling fears about pregnancy complications and abortion restrictions": https://catholicvoiceomaha.com/dispelling-fears-about-pregnancy-complications-and-abortion-restrictions/ ; Catholic Health Association, "Catholic Hospitals and Ectopic Pregnancies": https://chausa.org/publications/health-care-ethics-usa/article/winter-2011/catholic-hospitals-and-ectopic-pregnancies

Title: The Atomic Bomb
Dilemma: In August 1945, near the end of World War II, U.S. leaders decided to drop atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Historians' most credible estimates put the deaths by the end of 1945 at between about 110,000 and 210,000, most of them civilians. Defenders argued it would force a quick surrender and avoid an invasion that might have cost far more lives on both sides.
Question: Can destroying whole cities full of civilians be justified if it ends a war sooner and saves more lives overall?
Right Choice: Never target cities full of civilians
Wrong Choice: Drop the bombs to end the war faster
Catholic Answer: No. The Second Vatican Council taught, and the Catechism repeats: "Every act of war directed to the indiscriminate destruction of whole cities or vast areas with their inhabitants is a crime against God and man, which merits firm and unequivocal condemnation" (CCC 2314). The deliberate killing of non-combatants is always gravely wrong, even in a just war (CCC 2313). The cities also held military and industrial targets, and historians still debate the leaders' intentions and the bombs' part in Japan's surrender. The moral principle does not depend on that debate: destroying an entire city with its inhabitants is what CCC 2314 condemns, and when civilian deaths are meant to pressure an enemy into surrender, they are a means, not a side effect, so the principle of double effect cannot apply. "One may never do evil so that good may result from it" (CCC 1789). The Nagasaki bomb exploded over Urakami, the historic center of Nagasaki's Catholic community, and nearly destroyed its cathedral, which stood about 500 meters from the hypocenter. Visiting Hiroshima in 2019, Pope Francis declared that using atomic energy for war is immoral, and so is possessing nuclear weapons.
Key Principle: Deliberately targeting civilians is always a grave sin; a good end can never justify an evil means.
Sources: Pope Francis, Meeting for Peace, Hiroshima (24 November 2019): https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/speeches/2019/november/documents/papa-francesco_20191124_messaggio-incontropace-hiroshima.html ; Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes 80: http://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vatii_cons_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html ; Alex Wellerstein, "Counting the dead at Hiroshima and Nagasaki," Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists: https://thebulletin.org/2020/08/counting-the-dead-at-hiroshima-and-nagasaki/ ; UCA News, "Nagasaki Cathedral": https://www.ucanews.com/directory/pilgrimages/nagasaki-cathedral-a-testimony-of-persecution-and-atomic-bombing/244

Title: The Private Message
Dilemma: A friend sends you a private message about a personal problem she is going through. Another friend sees you reading it and asks to see it, just out of curiosity.
Question: Is it all right to show the message, since the second person is also your friend?
Right Choice: Keep it private unless your friend agrees
Wrong Choice: Show the message to satisfy the curiosity
Catholic Answer: No. What a friend confides to you is not yours to share. The Catechism teaches that "the good and safety of others, respect for privacy, and the common good are sufficient reasons for being silent about what ought not be known," and that "no one is bound to reveal the truth to someone who does not have the right to know it" (CCC 2489). Curiosity gives no one a right to know. Even information not given under a promise of secrecy "is not to be divulged without a grave and proportionate reason" (CCC 2491). If you think your friend needs help, ask her permission or encourage her to talk to someone she trusts. If her safety is at risk, getting help from a responsible adult comes first.
Key Principle: Respect for privacy: what is confided is shared only with permission, or for a grave reason.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Unverified Accusation
Dilemma: A post accusing a local coach of something serious is spreading online. It might be true, but no one has shown any evidence, and you do not know the people involved. A friend urges you to repost it "to warn people."
Question: Should you repost an accusation you cannot verify, if it might protect others?
Right Choice: Don't repost it; take real concerns to those responsible
Wrong Choice: Repost it to warn everyone
Catholic Answer: No. Spreading a serious accusation you cannot verify risks rash judgment, which "even tacitly, assumes as true, without sufficient foundation, the moral fault of a neighbor," and, if it is false, calumny, which "harms the reputation of others" (CCC 2477). "Everyone enjoys a natural right to the honor of his name and reputation" (CCC 2479), and online posts can do lasting damage that is very hard to repair (CCC 2487). Concern for others is good, so act on it responsibly: if you have real information about a danger, bring it privately to those responsible, such as parents, the school or club, or the police, who can look into it properly.
Key Principle: Protect people's good name: do not spread serious accusations you cannot verify.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The AI Essay
Dilemma: Your teacher allows spelling and grammar tools but says your essay must be your own work. A classmate shows you how an AI tool can write the whole essay in seconds, and says you could hand it in under your name.
Question: Is it honest to submit an essay written by AI as your own work?
Right Choice: Write it yourself, using only the tools the teacher allows
Wrong Choice: Hand in the AI's essay under your name
Catholic Answer: No. Handing in work as your own when it is not leads your teacher to believe something false about what you did. "To lie is to speak or act against the truth in order to lead someone into error" (CCC 2484). The virtue of truthfulness "consists in showing oneself true in deeds and truthful in words" (CCC 2468). It is also unfair to classmates who did their own work, and to a teacher who must grade fairly. Using a tool to brainstorm ideas or to explain a difficult concept is a different case: it can be honest help, as long as the teacher's rules allow it and the work you submit is truly yours. When in doubt, ask the teacher and be open about what you used.
Key Principle: Honesty: never present someone else's work, human or machine, as your own.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: Left Out on Purpose
Dilemma: Your friends are planning a group outing and deliberately leave out one classmate because they think she is awkward. You worry that if you object, the group will turn against you.
Question: Is going along with it harmless, since you are not the one being unkind?
Right Choice: Stand up for her kindly, and include her yourself
Wrong Choice: Go along with it to keep your place in the group
Catholic Answer: No. Deliberately shutting someone out to hurt or mock her is a failure in charity, and going along with it can make us share in it, since we cooperate in others' sins "by ordering, advising, praising, or approving them" (CCC 1868). "The duty of making oneself a neighbor to others and actively serving them becomes even more urgent when it involves the disadvantaged" (CCC 1932). You do not have to make a scene. Practical steps help: suggest including her, say you would rather everyone came, invite her to something yourself, or sit with her. It takes courage, which the Catechism calls fortitude, the virtue that "ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good" (CCC 1808).
Key Principle: Charity and courage: treat everyone with dignity, and take no part in excluding others.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Found Phone
Dilemma: You find a phone on a park bench. The screen is locked, but message previews keep popping up, and you could read them to try to work out whose it is.
Question: Is it all right to read the owner's private messages to find out who they are?
Right Choice: Return it without prying: use the emergency contact or hand it in
Wrong Choice: Read the messages to find out about the owner
Catholic Answer: You should make a real effort to return it, since the "deliberate retention of... objects lost" is against the Seventh Commandment (CCC 2409). But do it in a way that respects the owner's privacy: "everyone should observe an appropriate reserve concerning persons' private lives" (CCC 2492). Reading their messages goes far beyond what is needed. Respectful ways to return it: answer if someone calls it, use the emergency or medical contact many phones show on the lock screen, or hand it in to a nearby business, the park office, or the police. If you must look at the screen to find a contact, look only for that and nothing more.
Key Principle: Return what is lost, and respect the owner's privacy while doing it.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: Someone Else's Credit
Dilemma: A coworker quietly fixed a critical problem in your team's project the night before a deadline. At the meeting, your supervisor praises you for the result. Your coworker is not there to say anything.
Question: Is it all right to accept the praise, since you did not say anything false?
Right Choice: Thank the supervisor and say who really fixed it
Wrong Choice: Accept the praise and say nothing
Catholic Answer: Honesty is more than not saying false words. Letting a false impression stand to your own advantage, when you could easily correct it, misleads others: truthfulness "consists in showing oneself true in deeds and truthful in words, and in guarding against duplicity, dissimulation, and hypocrisy" (CCC 2468). It is also a matter of justice, the virtue that gives "their due to God and neighbor" (CCC 1807): the credit, and the good name that comes with it, belong to the one who earned them (CCC 2479). The fix is simple: say, kindly and without fuss, "Thank you, but it was actually my coworker who solved it."
Key Principle: Truth and justice: give others the credit they are due.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Alibi
Dilemma: A friend asks you to tell their parents they spent Saturday at your house, though they were somewhere else. They say they will get in big trouble if you refuse.
Question: Is it kind to lie to cover for a friend?
Right Choice: Refuse to lie, and encourage your friend to be honest
Wrong Choice: Tell the parents your friend was with you
Catholic Answer: No. "A lie consists in speaking a falsehood with the intention of deceiving" (CCC 2482), and a good motive such as helping a friend does not make it right: "the end does not justify the means" (CCC 1753). Kindness and deception are different things. Real friendship wants what is truly good for your friend, and covering for them could leave them in danger, since their parents need to know where they are. You can refuse warmly: tell your friend you care about them but will not lie, and encourage them to tell their parents the truth themselves. You do not have to volunteer everything you know, but you must not say what is false (CCC 2489).
Key Principle: Truthfulness: friendship never requires lying.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Group Chat Meme
Dilemma: Someone posts a humiliating meme about a student in a big group chat, and everyone is reacting with laughing emojis. You did not make it, but you are in the chat.
Question: Is adding a laughing reaction harmless, since you did not create the meme?
Right Choice: Don't join in; speak up or report it safely
Wrong Choice: Add a laughing reaction like everyone else
Catholic Answer: No. A reaction is a way of approving, and we share responsibility for others' sins when we cooperate in them "by ordering, advising, praising, or approving them" (CCC 1868). Mocking a person attacks "the honor of his name and reputation" (CCC 2479), and encouraging others to do wrong is scandal (CCC 2284). As a bystander, start by not joining in. Then do what is safe and proportionate: say something like "Not okay, take it down," message the person who posted it privately, report it to the platform or a responsible adult, and reach out to the student who was targeted.
Key Principle: Do not cooperate in harm: a bystander's approval adds to it.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Unsafe Shortcut
Dilemma: At work you discover that a shortcut your team has been taking could put customers or coworkers in danger. Reporting it will delay the project and frustrate your manager, who is under pressure to meet a deadline.
Question: Should you stay quiet to keep the project on schedule?
Right Choice: Report the risk through the proper channels
Wrong Choice: Stay quiet and let the shortcut continue
Catholic Answer: No. People's lives and safety come before convenience and deadlines. "The moral law prohibits exposing someone to mortal danger without grave reason, as well as refusing assistance to a person in danger" (CCC 2269), and we share responsibility for harm we fail to stop "when we have an obligation to do so" (CCC 1868). How you report it depends on how urgent the danger is and on your workplace's procedures. If someone could be hurt right away, act at once to stop it (warn people, stop the work, or call emergency services) and report it immediately. Otherwise, raise it honestly and respectfully, first with your manager, and, if that does not work, through your company's safety channels or the relevant authority. Loyal collaboration at work includes "the right, and at times the duty, to voice... just criticisms of that which seems harmful to the dignity of persons and to the good of the community" (CCC 2238).
Key Principle: Responsibility for others: protect people's safety, even at a cost to yourself.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Double Refund
Dilemma: You return an item to a store, and later notice that the store refunded your card twice. The amount is small, and you doubt anyone will ever notice.
Question: Can you keep the extra refund, since it was the store's mistake?
Right Choice: Tell the store and pay back the extra money
Wrong Choice: Keep it, since no one will notice
Catholic Answer: No. Money given in error still belongs to the store, and "any form of unjustly taking and keeping the property of others is against the seventh commandment" (CCC 2409). Justice requires restitution: those who have taken possession of the goods of another "are obliged to make restitution of them" (CCC 2412). A small amount makes the wrong less serious, but it does not make it right. Contact the store, explain the double refund, and arrange to pay it back. Being honest when no one would ever find out is where integrity is really formed.
Key Principle: Justice: return what was given to you by mistake.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: Forgiving Without Pretending
Dilemma: Someone keeps insulting you. Each time, he apologizes, and then does it again a few days later. Your friends say a good Christian should just forgive and put up with it.
Question: Does forgiving him mean pretending it is harmless and letting it continue?
Right Choice: Forgive him, and also set boundaries and get help to stop it
Wrong Choice: Pretend it is harmless and let it keep happening
Catholic Answer: Forgiveness is required of every Christian, and there is "no limit or measure" to it (CCC 2845). But forgiving is not pretending a wrong is harmless. "It is not in our power not to feel or to forget an offense; but the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion" (CCC 2843). You can forgive him from the heart, refuse to hold a grudge, and pray for him, while still telling him clearly to stop, keeping some distance, and asking a responsible person for help if it continues. Telling the truth about harm and protecting yourself are compatible with mercy; charity even includes "fraternal correction" (CCC 1829).
Key Principle: Mercy and truth: forgiveness does not require allowing harm to continue.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed

Title: The Family Budget
Dilemma: Money is tight in your family. Your parents promised you a new phone for your birthday next week. Then your younger brother breaks his glasses, and he cannot see in class without them. There is only enough money for one.
Question: Should you insist on the phone, since it was promised first?
Right Choice: Agree that his glasses come first
Wrong Choice: Insist on the phone, since it was promised first
Catholic Answer: Needs come before wants. The family is where members "learn to care and take responsibility for the young, the old, the sick, the handicapped, and the poor" (CCC 2208), and property is meant to help meet one's "basic needs and the needs of those in his charge" (CCC 2402). Glasses he cannot do without are a real need; a new phone is not. The fair way is to talk it over openly as a family: explain why the urgent need comes first, admit the disappointment, and plan together for the phone later. Generosity at home is where the habit of sharing begins.
Key Principle: Family responsibility: urgent needs come before wants.
Sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs listed
